accroche: The baby who learned to fear a rat has a laboratory name, and since 2009, two incompatible identities.
contenu_vulgarise:
Johns Hopkins, 1920. An eleven-month-old baby sits on a table, a white rat placed in front of him. He reaches out and touches it, with no sign of fear. John B. Watson and his assistant Rosalie Rayner try again, but this time a hammer strikes a steel bar just behind his head the moment he touches the animal. The din makes him jump and cry. A few sessions later, the rat alone is enough: the child turns away, cries, tries to crawl off the table.

## The Mechanism

This is the founding experiment of emotional conditioning in humans, published by Watson and Rayner in 1920 under the title “Conditioned Emotional Reactions.” The principle echoes that of Pavlov's dogs: pairing a neutral stimulus, the rat, with a stimulus that already triggers a reaction, the noise, which already frightens Albert, is enough, after a few repetitions, to transfer the reaction to the neutral stimulus.

Watson goes further: he tests generalization. Does the fear transfer to other objects that resemble the rat? Albert is frightened by a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat, and even a Santa Claus mask with a cotton beard: none of these had been paired with the noise. The fear had jumped from the rat to a whole category, “what is furry.”

The study has a single subject, no control group, and Albert leaves it before Watson could try to undo the conditioning: a mere logistical detail that forever prevents us from knowing whether the child grew up with a lasting fear or whether it faded on its own.

## What This Shifts

Nearly a century later, two teams try to find out what became of Albert, and arrive at two incompatible candidates. In 2009, Hall Beck, Sharman Levinson, and Gary Irons cross-reference the hospital's records and identify Albert as Douglas Merritte, the son of a wet nurse at the institution. In 2014, Russell Powell, Nancy Digdon, Ben Harris, and Christopher Smithson challenge that lead and propose William Albert Barger, born one day apart from Merritte, to another wet nurse at the same hospital.

The two lives could not be more different. Douglas Merritte dies at the age of six, afflicted with hydrocephalus. William Albert Barger dies in 2007 at 87; his niece reports that he did not like dogs, and the researchers conclude that he probably did not know he had been the subject of an experiment.

The uncertainty itself teaches more than its eventual resolution would. A founding experiment of twentieth-century psychology, cited in most textbooks, rests on a child whose identity has never been recorded anywhere in a verifiable way. What took place on that table in 1920 ended up better documented than the child himself.

repere.texte: The two lives proposed for “Albert” are opposed: Douglas Merritte dies at the age of six, afflicted with hydrocephalus; William Albert Barger dies in 2007 at 87, and his niece reports that he did not like dogs.
repere.source: Powell, Digdon, Harris & Smithson, “Correcting the Record on Watson, Rayner, and Little Albert,” American Psychologist, 2014

carte.punch: The baby from the fear laboratory never had a confirmed identity.
carte.idee: In 1920, Watson conditions an infant to fear a rat, then anything furry. Nearly a century later, two teams propose two different, incompatible children as being that baby, without ever settling the matter.

quiz.question: What does the generalization test carried out after Albert's conditioning to the rat show?
choix: That fear fades on its own without new reinforcement
That fear transfers to other objects that share a texture with the rat
That only the rat used for the conditioning still triggers fear
That fear can transfer only to animals, never to inanimate objects
quiz.explication: Albert is frightened by a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat, and a Santa Claus mask with a cotton beard, none of which had been paired with the noise: the fear went beyond the rat alone, to objects of the same texture, animals or not.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What methodological limitation affects Watson and Rayner's original 1920 study?
choix: A single subject, no control group, and a departure before any attempt at deconditioning
A sample of several hundred infants followed over ten years
A total absence of measurement of the fear reaction, which was only observed by the parents
A double-blind design that kept Watson from knowing which child received the noise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study covers only one child, with no control group, and Albert leaves the experiment before Watson could try to undo the conditioning, which makes it impossible to know what came next.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Beck, Levinson, and Irons identify in 2009 from the Johns Hopkins hospital records?
choix: That the Little Albert experiment never took place
William Albert Barger as the baby in the experiment
Douglas Merritte, the son of a wet nurse at the institution, as being Albert
A third candidate, unknown to later teams
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Beck, Levinson, and Irons cross-reference the hospital's records and identify Albert, in 2009, as Douglas Merritte, the son of a wet nurse at the institution.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the team of Powell, Digdon, Harris, and Smithson put forward in 2014 about Albert's identity?
choix: They confirm that Douglas Merritte is indeed the only valid candidate
They propose William Albert Barger, born one day apart from Merritte, to another wet nurse at the same hospital
They demonstrate that Albert never existed and that the study is a fraud
They place Albert's birth ten years after Watson's experiment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Powell, Digdon, Harris, and Smithson challenge the Merritte lead and in 2014 propose William Albert Barger, born one day apart, the son of another wet nurse at the same hospital.
